title: De Inventione
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
source: Translated by Claude from phi0474.phi036.perseus-lat2, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: fabula est, in qua nec verae nec veri similes res continentur, cuiusmodi est: Angues ingentes alites, iuncti iugo . historia est gesta res, ab aetatis nostrae memoria remota; quod genus: Appius indixit Carthaginiensibus bellum. argumentum est ficta res, quae tamen fieri potuit. huiusmodi apud Terentium: Nam is postquam excessit ex ephebis, Sosia. illa autem narratio, quae versatur in personis, eiusmodi est, ut in ea simul cum rebus ipsis personarum sermones et animi perspici possint, hoc modo: Venit ad me saepe clamitans: Quid agis, Micio?
passages.english: A fable is [a narrative] in which are contained things neither true nor probable, of this kind: "Huge winged snakes, joined to a yoke." History is an account of an action performed, remote from the memory of our age; of which kind is: "Appius declared war on the Carthaginians." A plot (*argumentum*) is a fictitious event which nevertheless could have happened. Of this kind is [the passage] in Terence: "For after he had left the ranks of the youths, Sosia." But that narrative which is concerned with persons is of such a kind that in it, together with the events themselves, the conversations and minds of the persons can be seen, in this way: "He comes to me, constantly shouting: 'What are you doing, Micio?'"
passages.notes: The verse quotations are from Pacuvius (?) (the snakes), Terence's Andria ("For after he had left...") and Terence's Adelphoe ("He comes to me..."). *Argumentum* here means a realistic fictional plot, as in comedy.

passages.original: Atque his de partitione praeceptis in omni dictione meminisse oportebit, ut et prima quaeque pars, ut exposita est in partitione, sic ordine transigatur et omnibus explicatis peroratum sit hoc modo, ut ne quid posterius praeter conclusionem inferatur. partitur apud Terentium breviter et commode senex in Andria, quae cognoscere libertum velit: Eo pacto et gnati vitam et consilium meum Cognosces et quid facere in hac re te velim. itaque quemadmodum in partitione proposuit, ita narrat, primum nati vitam: Nam is postquam excessit ex ephebis ; deinde suum consilium: Et nunc id operam do .
passages.english: And with these precepts about partition, it will be necessary to remember in every speech both that each part, in the order in which it was set out in the partition, should be dealt with in that order, and that, when everything has been explained, the speech should be concluded in such a way that nothing further is brought in except the conclusion. The old man in Terence's Andria makes his partition briefly and aptly, [setting out] what he wants his freedman to learn: "In this way you will learn both my son's life and my plan, and what I want you to do in this matter." And so, just as he proposed in the partition, so he narrates: first his son's life, "For after he had left the ranks of the youths"; then his own plan, "And now I am taking pains over this."
passages.notes: *partitio* is the rhetorical division in which the speaker lists the points he will treat.

passages.original: Inductio est oratio, quae rebus non dubiis captat assensionem eius, quicum instituta est; quibus assensionibus facit, ut illi dubia quaedam res propter similitudinem earum rerum, quibus assensit, probetur; velut apud Socraticum Aeschinen demonstrat Socrates cum Xenophontis uxore et cum ipso Xenophonte Aspasiam locutam: dic mihi, quaeso, Xenophontis uxor, si vicina tua melius habeat aurum, quam tu habes, utrum illudne an tuum malis?illud, inquit. quid, si vestem et ceterum ornatum muliebrem pretii maioris habeat, quam tu habes, tuumne an illius malis?
passages.english: Induction is a form of argument which, by means of things not in doubt, wins the assent of the person with whom it is undertaken; and by these assents it brings it about that some doubtful matter is approved by him because of its similarity to the things to which he has assented. So, for example, in the Socratic Aeschines, Socrates shows that Aspasia spoke with Xenophon's wife and with Xenophon himself: "Tell me, please, wife of Xenophon, if your neighbour has finer gold than you have, would you prefer hers or yours?" "Hers," she said. "What if she has clothing and other feminine adornment of greater value than you have, would you prefer yours or hers?"
passages.notes: 'The Socratic Aeschines' is Aeschines of Sphettus, author of Socratic dialogues (here apparently his Aspasia). 'malis?illud' is run together in the text and has been read as 'malis? illud'.

passages.original: aut si, cum totum debebit ostendere, de parte aliqua loquatur, hoc modo: Mulierum genus avarum est; nam Eriphyla auro viri vitam vendidit; aut si non id, quod accusabitur, defendet, ut, si qui, cum ambitus accusabitur, manu se fortem esse defendet; aut ut Amphion apud Euripidem, item apud Pacuvium, qui vituperata musica sapientiam laudat; aut si res ex hominis vitio vituperabitur, ut, si qui doctrinam ex alicuius docti vitiis reprehendat; aut si qui, cum aliquem volet laudare, de felicitate eius, non de virtute dicat;
passages.english: or if, when he ought to show the whole, he speaks about some part, in this way: 'The female sex is greedy; for Eriphyle sold her husband's life for gold'; or if he defends not what he is accused of, as if someone, when accused of electoral bribery, should defend himself by saying he is brave in combat; or like Amphion in Euripides, and likewise in Pacuvius, who, when music has been disparaged, praises wisdom; or if a thing is censured on account of a person's fault, as if someone should criticise learning from the faults of some learned man; or if someone, when he wants to praise somebody, speaks of his good fortune and not of his virtue;

passages.original: aut si, cum de certa re quaeretur, de communi instituetur oratio, ut, si quis, cum aliqui deliberent, bellum gerant an non, pacem laudet omnino, non illud bellum inutile esse demonstret; aut si ratio alicuius rei reddetur falsa, hoc modo: pecunia bonum est, propterea quod ea maxime vitam beatam efficiat; aut infirma, ut Plautus: Amicum castigare ob meritam noxiam, Immune est facinus; verum in aetate utile Et conducibile; nam ego amicum hodie meum Concastigabo pro commerita noxia; aut eadem, hoc modo: malum est avaritia; multos enim magnis incommodis affecit pecuniae cupiditas; aut parum idonea, hoc modo: maximum bonum est amicitia;
passages.english: Or if, when a specific matter is being inquired into, the speech is directed to a general one: for example, if, when some people are deliberating whether to wage war or not, someone were to praise peace in general, and not show that that particular war is disadvantageous; or if a false reason is given for something, in this way: "Money is a good, because it above all produces a happy life"; or a weak one, as in Plautus: "To rebuke a friend for a deserved offence is a thankless deed; but at times it is useful and profitable; for today I shall rebuke my friend for his well-deserved offence"; or the same [as the claim], in this way: "Avarice is an evil; for the desire for money has afflicted many with great harm"; or one not sufficiently apt, in this way: "Friendship is the greatest good;
passages.notes: The Plautus quotation is from Trinummus. "Immune" is taken in the sense of "thankless"/"unrewarding"; this sense is uncertain. "The same" means a reason that merely restates the claim.
